strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important problem: the lack of functional grounding in XAI evaluation, and the framing of explanations as 'a means to an end' is compelling and clearly motivated.

The decision-theoretic formalization (Definitions 1-3) provides a coherent vocabulary and a useful forcing function that requires researchers to specify action space, state space, utility, and data-generating distribution for a use case.

Proposition 7 (explanations are a garbling of features and predictions and thus give no value to an idealized rational agent) is a clean and correct insight that usefully bounds what explanations can be expected to do and clarifies why any benefit must come from human deviation from idealized behavior.

The three-level decomposition (theoretic, human-complementary, behavioral value) offers a sensible conceptual workflow that spans theoretical and empirical perspectives, and the discussion of how to interpret magnitudes is thoughtful.

The related-work section is well-positioned and the limitations discussion (Section 5) is honest, explicitly acknowledging settings where decision theory is ill-equipped to quantify explanation value (future-based or idiosyncratic decisions).
weaknesses: The central technical result (Proposition 7) is a direct corollary of Blackwell's informativeness theorem (restated as Theorem 8); the 'proof' is essentially a one-line garbling argument, so the theoretical novelty is limited.

The paper's core claim — that this framework improves the design and evaluation of explanations — is asserted rather than demonstrated. No real human study is conducted, and the only empirical illustration (Appendix B) uses a synthetic linear model as a stand-in for human predictions, which cannot support claims about human-complementary or behavioral value.

The behavioral value of explanation (Definition 13) is defined but never estimated; the paper claims behavioral evaluation 'must ultimately be conducted' but provides no evidence that the proposed workflow yields actionable results.

The informal analysis of misinformed/misoptimizing/uninformed agents (Section 3.2) is heuristic and unvalidated. The paper demands that new XAI methods be accompanied by 'a model of the expected use of the information by an agent,' yet does not supply such a model itself, leaving the mechanism claims unsubstantiated.

Technical sloppiness in places: Eqs. (5)-(6) and the 'softmax' operator in Eq. (7) are loosely defined; the deterministic-explanation assumption underlying Proposition 7 (Z = E(X, Y)) is restrictive and its relaxation is not discussed; the coarsening algorithm in Appendix A claims a 2-approximation and O(log|V*|) complexity without proof or empirical validation.

Originality concerns: the framework substantially overlaps with prior work the authors themselves cite (Guo et al. [26,27] on decision-theoretic reliance and value of information; Wu et al. [61] on the rational agent benchmark). The contribution is largely a synthesis and extension rather than a new method or new theoretical understanding.

Reproducibility is weak: the single demonstration uses one dataset (Ames) with simulated human labels, so the empirical section neither tests the framework against real decision-makers nor provides a benchmark others can build on.

strengths: The paper offers a coherent and clearly motivated decision-theoretic framing of explanation evaluation. Casting explanations as information signals and defining theoretic, human-complementary, and behavioral value of explanation provides a useful conceptual scaffolding for thinking about when explanations can help.

Proposition 7 and the garbling argument are technically correct: because post-hoc explanations are (in the authors' definition) deterministic functions of features and model prediction, they add no information to an idealized Bayesian agent, so any benefit must arise from bounded rationality. This is a valuable, if not new, clarification that sharpens the discussion of why explanations can help imperfect agents.

The coarsening procedure in Appendix A is a sensible practical attempt to prevent the rational-agent benchmark from overfitting when signals are high-dimensional, and the discussion of its implications for study design (the coarsened signal must be used in the user study) is thoughtful.

The related-work discussion is broad and the limitations section (Section 5) honestly acknowledges cases where decision theory is ill-equipped to quantify explanation value, engaging with counterarguments rather than dismissing them.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. Definitions 9, 11, and 13 and the reliance/decision-theoretic evaluation framing substantially overlap with the authors' own earlier work (Guo et al. [26], [27]); the text explicitly says it is "adapting the approach of [26]." Proposition 7 restates a well-known garbling result. The incremental contribution over existing decision-theoretic treatments of human-AI reliance is modest for a top venue.

Weak empirical grounding for the central practical claim. The only demonstration (Appendix B) uses a *synthetic* human decision-maker (a linear model, Eq. 10) on a 3-feature toy task. The observed results are essentially guaranteed by construction—the synthetic "human" is a linear function of the same features, so the simulation simply recapitulates the theory. There is no real user study and no evaluation of actual XAI methods on real decision tasks, so the claim that the framework helps design and evaluate explanations in practice (clinical support, recourse, debugging) is not evidenced. The use cases in Examples 4-6 are asserted, not evaluated.

Definition 11 ("potential complementary value of explanation") does not involve the explanation Z at all—it measures the value of features X given human predictions (R_{Ŷᴴ∪X} − R_{Ŷᴴ}). Naming this the value of the *explanation* is misleading, and consequently the demonstration (Example 12, Figure 1) never computes an explanation-specific quantity; it computes the value of features/human predictions. This blurs the paper's central object of study.

The formalism is more restrictive than claimed. Defining ℰ: 𝒴 × 𝒳 → 𝒵 excludes global explanations, inherently interpretable models, and any explanation that depends on model internals beyond a single prediction—yet Section 2 asserts these are all covered. If explanations could carry information about the model beyond (X, Ŷ), the garbling argument (and hence Proposition 7) would not hold, so the claimed generality is unsupported and Proposition 7 becomes close to vacuous for the stated scope.

Sloppy formalism in the bounded-rationality models. Adding Gaussian noise to posterior distributions (p^mis = p^opt + ξ) does not yield a valid probability distribution (may be negative, need not sum to one), and the misoptimizing-agent rule a(v) = a^failopt(v)·p(ŷ≠s|ŷ,z) + ŷ·p(ŷ=s|ŷ,z) mixes actions and labels in a way that is not well defined. These are presented as illustrative, but they undercut the rigor the paper claims to bring.

Unproven technical claims in Appendix A. The assertions that the coarsening algorithm yields a 2-factor approximation (|V'| ≥ ½|V*|) and runs in O(log(|V*|)) time are stated without proof and are not obviously correct from the halving procedure described.

Presentation problems throughout: numerous typos and grammatical errors ("Practitioners in other disciplines rely on them methods," "This definition formalizes an use case," "misoptimzing"), inconsistent terminology ("theoretic" vs. "theoretical value"), inconsistent heading/bullet formatting (e.g., Definition 1), and occasional notational sloppiness (the conditioning in Eq. 2). No code or artifact release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility even of the toy demonstration.

strengths: Well-motivated and coherent thesis: the paper convincingly argues that explanations should be treated as *means* to a specified decision end, and operationalizes this via statistical decision theory. The framing of explanations as information signals within a decision task (Definitions 1–3) is clean and useful.

Proposition 7 is a correct and clarifying result: by leveraging Blackwell's informativeness theorem and the 'garbling' argument, the paper shows that explanations which are deterministic functions of X and Ŷ add no value to an idealized rational Bayesian agent. This is a valuable conceptual point that sharpens why explanations can only help boundedly-rational humans.

The three definitions of value of explanation (theoretic Δ_E, human-complementary Δ_E_compl, behavioral Δ_E_behavioral) provide an actionable evaluation workflow: check theoretical potential and complementarity before running costly user studies. The observations that Δ_E_behavioral can be negative or can exceed Δ_E are insightful and non-obvious.

Good scholarly positioning: the paper engages substantively with related work (Chen et al., Fok & Weld, Guo et al., signaling theory, value-of-information), and its critique of fidelity/local-accuracy validation is well-supported.

Appendix A's procedure for estimating the data-generating distribution with an explicit coarsening step is a thoughtful practical contribution, and the caveat that coarsened signals must be used consistently in downstream user studies shows careful reasoning about pitfalls.
The diverse worked examples (medical treatment, recourse, feature selection, home pricing) illustrate that the framework can span multiple use cases, which supports the paper's generality claim.
The writing is clear and the argumentative structure is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The empirical demonstration is weak and largely circular. It relies on a synthetic 'human' (a linear model fit on the training labels, Eq. 10) rather than real decision-makers. Because the synthetic predictions are generated by a function of the features, the plotted results (Figure 1) largely confirm Proposition 7 by construction. No estimate of the behavioral value of explanation (Definition 13) is provided, so the framework's central behavioral claim remains untested.

Definition 9 labels Δ_E = R_X − R_∅ the 'theoretic value of explanation,' but this quantity does not depend on the explanation at all—it is the value of the features. It is an upper bound on what an explanation could unlock, not a measure of the explanation. Similarly, Definition 11 measures the value of features given human predictions rather than of the explanation itself, which the authors acknowledge but which makes the naming misleading and muddles the conceptual distinction among the three quantities.

Limited technical novelty. Proposition 7 is a direct application of Blackwell's garbling result, and Definitions 9/11/13 are adaptations of standard value-of-information and ATE. The contribution is primarily conceptual and organizational rather than a new method or theorem.

The framework is not fully operationalized. The pivotal object—the model of expected explanation use by an agent—is discussed only qualitatively via misinformed/misoptimizing/uninformed archetypes; no concrete instantiation is specified, estimated, or validated. The use-case examples (Examples 4–6, 10) are illustrative sketches rather than worked-out analyses, so the claimed breadth is asserted more than demonstrated.

Despite claiming applicability to 'clinical decision support, providing recourse, or debugging,' only a single task (home pricing) is analyzed, and only in the appendix with synthetic data. The debugging and recourse use cases receive no quantitative treatment.
Reproducibility is not adequately addressed: there is no mention of code or data release, and the synthetic experiment is described only briefly, making independent verification difficult.

strengths: Provides a coherent decision-theoretic framework for evaluating explanations as information signals, with clear estimands (theoretic value, human-complementary value, behavioral value) that tie explanation value to decision performance.
Formalizes the intuition that deterministic explanations cannot improve a rational agent's expected utility (Proposition 1), grounding the need for bounded rationality assumptions.
Decomposes theoretic value into independent and contextual components, enabling comparison of explanation methods and diagnostic interpretation of human-AI study results.
Offers a practical validation workflow, including a coarsening algorithm to estimate rational benchmarks in high-dimensional settings.
Demonstrates the framework across multiple domains: medical decision-making, reanalysis of human-AI decision support studies, and mechanistic interpretability alignment auditing.

Reanalysis of prior human-AI studies shows consistency between estimated theoretical values and observed behavioral effects, illustrating the framework's potential to explain why explanations fail or succeed.
weaknesses: The coarsening algorithm (Algorithm 1) selects the clustering that maximizes R_all on the full dataset while only constraining the train-test gap, which risks optimistic bias in the estimated rational benchmarks and undermines the validity of all theoretical value estimates.

The mechanistic interpretability demonstration uses an LLM (Qwen3-14B) to simulate human decisions, so the reported 'behavioral value' is not evidence about human behavior; the claim to interpret behavioral effects in mechanistic interpretability is therefore not supported by human data.

For the deception detection reanalysis, the original explanations shown to humans were unavailable, so the authors regenerate explanations following instructions. The theoretical values computed on regenerated explanations may not correspond to the actual explanations used in the human study, weakening the comparison between theoretical predictions and behavioral outcomes.

The human-complementary value is defined using a rational agent that observes human decisions, which is a theoretical upper bound but not a direct measure of how much explanations can complement human decision-making; it may overstate the actionable value of explanations.
No code or data release is mentioned, and the algorithm contains ambiguities/typos (e.g., line 16 posterior formula, garbling constraints not enforced), making reproducibility difficult.

The paper lacks sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters (clustering grid, tolerance δ) and does not report uncertainty for the theoretical benchmarks, despite the estimates' dependence on the coarsening procedure.
Presentation is dense and contains numerous grammatical/typographical errors (e.g., 'as as', 'explantions', 'SEA' for SAE), which hinder readability and reproducibility.

The theoretical value Δ_E is not explanation-specific (it depends only on the decision problem), so the framework's first stage does not evaluate the explanation method itself; this is acknowledged but limits the direct utility for comparing explanation techniques.

strengths: The decision-theoretic framing of explanations as information signals valued by expected decision improvement is a genuinely useful conceptual move that directly addresses the well-documented critique that explanation evaluation relies on proxy properties (faithfulness, robustness, self-reported understanding) weakly tied to practice. The three-stage workflow (theoretic → human-complementary → behavioral) is a coherent and actionable validation protocol.

Proposition 1 is a clean and correct negative result: since Z = E(X, Ŷ) is a deterministic function of X and Ŷ, it is a garbling, so R_{X∪Ŷ∪Z} = R_{X∪Ŷ}. This insight usefully reframes the field's implicit assumption that explanations help rational agents, and motivates the bounded-rationality account in Appendix E.

The decomposition of explanation value into independent vs. contextual components (Defs. 4-5, 7-8) is a helpful diagnostic that separates the information conveyed directly by the explanation from the information the explanation helps the user 'unlock' in the features.

The framework is theoretically grounded—Blackwell informativeness, the equivalence of utility functions and proper scoring rules, and the robust worst-case analysis over V-shaped scoring rules (Appendix D) give it a principled backbone.

The retrospective re-analysis of the Lai & Tan and Bansal et al. studies using real human decisions (Section 5.1) is the strongest empirical demonstration and produces a plausible, non-trivial interpretation of why deception-detection explanations helped while sentiment explanations did not.
weaknesses: The headline estimand Δ_E = R_X − R_∅ is not explanation-specific; the authors concede this ('Δ_E is not explanation specific: it depends only on the target decision problem'). The central 'theoretic value of explanation' therefore does not evaluate any explanation at all—it evaluates the decision problem—which undercuts the claim of a framework for explanation evaluation.

The behavioral-value results for the mechanistic interpretability experiment (Table 2) are obtained by prompting an LLM (Qwen3-14B) to simulate human decisions, not from human subjects. This cannot support the paper's definition of behavioral value as 'the causal effect of providing the explanation to human decision-makers' (Definition 9).

In the medical example, the 'human decisions' A^H are produced by a rule-based classifier over radiology reports, not by humans. Consequently the reported 'human-complementary value' is not human-complementary value, and the claim that humans fail to extract explanation information is untested.

The retrospective re-analyses re-generate explanations rather than using those actually shown to participants ('the dataset does not provide the specific explanations displayed to the human decision-maker'). The behavioral values in Table 1 are thus not the causal effects of the explanations the human subjects saw, weakening the claim that the framework explains the observed study outcomes.

Empirical estimation rests on an ad hoc coarsening procedure (Algorithm 1) using grid search over cluster counts and a tolerance δ to suppress overfitting. The resulting benchmarks are sensitive to clustering choices with no principled guarantee, and the garbling-preservation constraints (Eqs. 7-8) are stated but difficult to enforce in practice (Eq. 8 also appears to contain a typo, referencing f_1).

The 'revelation through action' assumption—treating baseline human decisions A^H as a signal to a rational agent to form R_{A^H}—conflates decision quality with information content. R_{A^H} can be inflated by mere correlation between human actions and the state even when humans carry no decision-relevant information, biasing Δ_E_compl.

The interpretation of the sentiment-classification results is partly circular: the framework's 'pre-study prediction' that explanations would not help is derived from the same (regenerated) explanations and decisions used to explain the study outcome, so it is post hoc rather than a genuine prospective validation.

The core machinery is inherited from prior work (Wu et al.'s rational agent benchmark; Guo et al.'s decision-theoretic framework for AI reliance). The incremental novelty—the explanation-specific framing and the independent/contextual decomposition—is modest, and Proposition 1 is a fairly direct application of the data-processing/Blackwell garbling property.

Presentation is uneven: the abstract's description of a 'theoretical benchmark that upper-bounds achievable performance by any agent with the explanation' is misleading given that R_X is features-only and Proposition 1 implies explanations add nothing for a rational agent; figures are cluttered and hard to read; and Appendix E's account of how explanations help boundedly rational agents is asserted informally rather than established by formal results, despite being central to justifying the framework.

There is no honest limitations section acknowledging the proxy nature of the 'human' decisions (LLM-simulated and rule-based) or the ad hoc nature of the coarsening estimator; the Impact Statement flatly asserts no negative consequences, which is naive for a paper whose central message could be read as 'explanations are worthless to rational agents.'

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap in XAI evaluation: it moves beyond proxy properties like faithfulness and self-reported understanding toward decision-theoretic value on a specified task, formalizing explanations as information signals.

It provides a clear formal setup using Bayesian rational agents, expected utility, and Blackwell informativeness; Proposition 1's result that deterministic explanations are garbling of X and Y is a valuable conceptual clarification.

The three estimands (theoretic, human-complementary, behavioral) and their independent/contextual decompositions offer a useful diagnostic workflow for asking whether explanations can help, whether human baselines already capture the relevant information, and whether deployment causally improves decisions.
The framework connects to proper scoring rules and robust analysis over V-shaped scoring rules, which helps address utility ambiguity and links to Blackwell order.
The empirical demonstrations span medical decision making, reanalysis of prior human-AI studies, and mechanistic interpretability, illustrating how the framework can be applied and interpreted.

The reanalysis of deception detection and sentiment classification provides post hoc insight into when explanations did or did not help, and the coarsening algorithm addresses an important practical problem of overfitting high-dimensional rational-agent benchmarks.
Limitations are discussed, including unobserved private information, ambiguous utilities, and boundedly rational agents.
weaknesses: The first two estimands are not explanation-specific: Delta_E = R_X - R_empty depends only on the decision problem, and Delta_E_compl = R_X - R_{A^H} does not involve Z at all. Only the decomposition component Delta_ind-E_compl and the behavioral value directly evaluate an explanation, so the framework's ability to validate explanations at the theoretic/complementary stages is more limited than the framing suggests.

The coarsening approach in Algorithm 1 is heuristic and lacks theoretical guarantees. It depends on unspecified clustering choices, cluster-count grids, and a tolerance delta; the resulting R_X is an upper bound only for the coarsened signal, not the original signal. This makes the practical estimation of the estimands fragile and potentially sensitive to hyperparameters.

Empirical validation is weak for human decision support. The medical 'human decisions' are induced by a rule-based model on radiology reports, not actual human decisions. In the deception/sentiment reanalysis, the specific explanations shown to participants were not available and were regenerated, so the estimated information model may not match the actual treatment. In the mechanistic interpretability demonstration, 'human decisions' are simulated with Qwen3-14B, so the behavioral value is not evidence about human decision-makers.

There is no prospective study showing that the workflow predicts explanation effectiveness or improves explanation selection. The claim that the framework would have predicted the sentiment results is retrospective, and the reanalysis cannot establish practical utility.

The upper-bound logic has an unresolved inconsistency: Definition 6 uses R_X as the upper bound, but the paper acknowledges that if humans have private information not in X, R_X may not upper-bound human-relevant performance. The proposed check R_{X_AI union A^H} > R_{X_AI} is not integrated into the formal estimands.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned, clustering algorithm details are missing, hyperparameter grids vary across experiments, and the LLM-simulated study depends on model version/prompt choices. MIMIC access is restricted, further limiting replication.

Presentation could be improved: there are typos and notation inconsistencies (e.g., 'as as', 'of of', 'explantions', 'SEA' instead of SAE, R_varnothing vs R_emptyset), and some figures/definitions would benefit from clearer exposition.

Limitations and ethics discussion is brief. The impact statement dismisses negative consequences without discussing risks of treating LLM-simulated decisions as human proxies or of using decision-theoretic evaluation to justify harmful or manipulative explanations.
